feedback: A is correct because paracetamol is normally metabolised by glucuronidation and sulfation. In overdose, these pathways are saturated, and the cytochrome P450 system produces N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI). NAPQI is toxic but is usually detoxified by glutathione. Once glutathione stores are depleted, NAPQI binds covalently to hepatocyte cellular proteins, causing centrilobular necrosis. C is incorrect as CYP induction (e.g., by alcohol) increases toxicity but is not the mechanism of the injury itself.

question:
A 34 year old woman from Southeast Asia is screened for hepatitis B during her first pregnancy. 

Investigations:
Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg): Positive
Hepatitis B e-antigen (HBeAg): Positive
Anti-HBc IgG: Positive
Anti-HBs: Negative

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.B: Chronic Hepatitis B infection with high infectivity
options.C: Chronic Hepatitis B infection with low infectivity
options.D: Immunity due to previous natural infection

feedback: B is correct. The presence of HBsAg for more than 6 months (implied chronic status by IgG anti-HBc and epidemiological context) indicates chronic infection. HBeAg is a marker of high viral replication and thus high infectivity. Acute infection would typically show IgM anti-HBc. Immunity (D and E) would require a positive Anti-HBs and negative HBsAg. Low infectivity (C) would be indicated by the presence of Anti-HBe instead of HBeAg.

question:
A 29 year old man attends the GP for a review of his hepatitis B status. He was diagnosed 8 months ago during a routine screen. He is currently asymptomatic and his physical examination is unremarkable.

Investigations:
Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg): Positive
Hepatitis B e-antigen (HBeAg): Positive
Anti-HBc IgG: Positive
Anti-HBc IgM: Negative
ALT: 48 U/L (10–40)

What is the most likely state of his infection?
feedback: B is correct because the presence of HBsAg for more than 6 months defines chronic infection, and HBeAg positivity indicates high viral replication and infectivity. A is incorrect because Anti-HBc IgM would be positive in acute infection. C is incorrect because low infectivity would typically be marked by HBeAg negativity and Anti-HBe positivity. D and E are incorrect because HBsAg would be negative in immune individuals.

question:
A 42 year old woman presents to the medical clinic with a 3-month history of worsening fatigue and joint pains. On examination, she has mild scleral icterus and several spider naevi on her chest.

Investigations:
Bilirubin: 42 µmol/L (<21)
ALT: 385 U/L (10–40)
ALP: 115 U/L (30–130)
Albumin: 34 g/L (35–50)
Antinuclear antibody (ANA): Positive (1:160)
Anti-smooth muscle antibody (ASMA): Positive

What is the most likely diagnosis?
feedback: A is correct because the patient presents with a 'hepatitic' picture (disproportionately raised ALT), hyperbilirubinaemia, and positive ANA/ASMA, which are classic for Type 1 Autoimmune Hepatitis. B is incorrect as there is no risk factor mentioned and the autoantibodies point elsewhere. C is incorrect as ALT is usually only mildly elevated. D is incorrect as it typically presents with a 'cholestatic' pattern (very high ALP). E is incorrect as it usually presents in younger patients with neurological features or Kayser-Fleischer rings.

question:
A 64 year old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 1-week history of jaundice and malaise. He has not travelled outside of the UK in the last 10 years. He mentions he recently attended a local agricultural fair where he consumed rare-cooked pork sausages.

Investigations:
Bilirubin: 88 µmol/L (<21)
ALT: 1450 U/L (10–40)
ALP: 180 U/L (30–130)

Which virus is the most likely cause of his presentation?
feedback: E is correct because Hepatitis E (specifically genotype 3 in the UK) is increasingly common and often transmitted through undercooked pork (zoonosis). A is incorrect as it is more commonly associated with travel or specific outbreaks. B and C are primarily bloodborne. D only occurs as a co-infection or super-infection with Hepatitis B.

question:
A 35 year old man is found to be positive for Hepatitis C antibodies during screening at a drug recovery centre. He used intravenous drugs 10 years ago but has been abstinent since. Further testing confirms the presence of HCV RNA in his blood.

What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.C: Monitoring of LFTs every 6 months only

feedback: D is correct because direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) are now the standard of care for chronic Hepatitis C, offering high cure rates with minimal side effects. A and B are incorrect as interferon and ribavirin monotherapy are outdated and less effective. C is incorrect because chronic HCV with detectable RNA requires treatment to prevent cirrhosis. E is incorrect as transplantation is reserved for end-stage liver disease or hepatocellular carcinoma.

subtopic: Infection of the gastrointestinal and liver systems
question:
A 48 year old man presents to his GP with a six-week history of epigastric burning that is worse when he is hungry. He has no weight loss, dysphagia, or vomiting. He has been taking over-the-counter omeprazole 20mg daily for the last month, which provides partial relief. The GP suspects a peptic ulcer caused by Helicobacter pylori and wishes to perform a non-invasive test.

Which of the following is the most appropriate instruction to give the patient to ensure an accurate test result?

options.A: Perform a stool antigen test immediately
options.B: Perform a carbon-13 urea breath test immediately
options.C: Switch the omeprazole to ranitidine for 1 week then perform a urea breath test
options.D: Stop the omeprazole for 24 hours before a stool antigen test

feedback: To ensure the accuracy of non-invasive Helicobacter pylori tests (such as the stool antigen test or the carbon-13 urea breath test), patients must stop taking Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs) like omeprazole for at least 2 weeks. Antibiotics should be stopped for 4 weeks. PPIs can suppress the bacteria and lead to false-negative results.

options_corrected.A: Perform a stool antigen test immediately
options_corrected.B: Perform a carbon-13 urea breath test immediately
options_corrected.C: Stop the omeprazole for 2 weeks before a stool antigen test
options_corrected.D: Stop the omeprazole for 24 hours before a stool antigen test
options_corrected.E: Switch the omeprazole to ranitidine for 1 week then perform a urea breath test

subtopic: Infection of the gastrointestinal and liver systems
question:
A 19 year old university student presents to the Emergency Department with a two-day history of profuse diarrhoea, which has become bloody over the last 12 hours. He reports severe periumbilical cramping and a headache. He attended a student barbecue five days ago where he recalls the chicken was slightly undercooked. 

On examination, his temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate is 102 bpm, and blood pressure is 118/76 mmHg. 

Investigations:
White cell count: 12.8 x 10^9/L (4.0–11.0)
Hemoglobin: 142 g/L (130–175)
Sodium: 138 mmol/L (135–145)
Potassium: 4.1 mmol/L (3.5–5.0)
Creatinine: 82 µmol/L (60–120)

Which organism is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
feedback: Campylobacter jejuni is the most common bacterial cause of gastroenteritis in the UK. It is frequently associated with undercooked poultry. The incubation period is typically 2-5 days, and it often presents with severe abdominal pain, fever, and bloody diarrhoea. Bacillus cereus and S. aureus usually cause rapid-onset vomiting (1-6 hours). Norovirus causes watery diarrhoea and vomiting, and Cholera causes 'rice-water' stools with profound dehydration.

subtopic: Infection of the gastrointestinal and liver systems
question:
A 28 year old woman presents to the GP after returning from a trekking holiday in Southeast Asia. She has had greasy, foul-smelling diarrhoea and significant abdominal bloating for the past 10 days. She has not seen any blood in her stool. She feels tired but is otherwise well.

Investigations:
Sodium: 139 mmol/L (135–145)
Potassium: 3.9 mmol/L (3.5–5.0)
Creatinine: 70 µmol/L (60–120)

Stool microscopy reveals the presence of trophozoites with a 'pear-shape' and two nuclei. 

Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment for this patient?
feedback: The clinical presentation (bloating, greasy stools, travel) and microscopy (pear-shaped trophozoites) are classic for Giardia lamblia infection. The first-line treatment for giardiasis is metronidazole (or tinidazole). Ciprofloxacin is used for bacterial causes like Shigella, and Vancomycin is used for C. difficile.

subtopic: Infection of the gastrointestinal and liver systems
question:
A 55 year old woman is diagnosed with a duodenal ulcer. A biopsy taken during an Oesophago-Gastro-Duodenoscopy (OGD) is positive for the rapid urease test (CLO test), confirming Helicobacter pylori infection. She has no known drug allergies and has never been treated for this infection before.

According to UK guidelines (NICE), which of the following represents the standard first-line eradication therapy?
feedback: Standard first-line 'triple therapy' for H. pylori eradication in the UK typically consists of a Proton Pump Inhibitor (PPI) like omeprazole, plus two antibiotics (usually Amoxicillin and either Clarithromycin or Metronidazole) taken for 7 days. This combination is necessary to overcome resistance and ensure eradication.

question:
A 48 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department after vomiting a large amount of 'coffee-ground' material. He has a history of heavy alcohol consumption and smokes 20 cigarettes a day. On examination, he is alert. Pulse is 88 bpm, BP is 128/82 mmHg, and his respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute.

Investigations:
Haemoglobin: 118 g/L (130–175)
Urea: 9.2 mmol/L (2.5–7.8)
Creatinine: 82 µmol/L (60–120)

Which clinical scoring system should be used at this point to assess his risk of requiring an intervention or his risk of mortality?
feedback: C is correct because the Glasgow-Blatchford Score (GBS) is the recommended tool for initial risk assessment in patients presenting with an upper gastrointestinal bleed before endoscopy. It identifies patients who are at low risk and may be suitable for outpatient management. E is incorrect because the Rockall Score is primarily used after endoscopy to assess the risk of re-bleeding and mortality. A is for liver cirrhosis severity, B is for pneumonia, and D is for bleeding risk in patients on anticoagulants.

question:
A 72 year old woman is admitted to the hospital with a two-day history of passing black, tarry, foul-smelling stools. She has a history of osteoarthritis for which she takes naproxen daily. She denies any previous history of dyspepsia or weight loss. On examination, she has mild epigastric tenderness but no signs of chronic liver disease.

Investigations:
Haemoglobin: 92 g/L (115–150)
Mean Cell Volume (MCV): 86 fL (80–96)

Which is the most likely cause of her gastrointestinal bleeding?
feedback: E is correct because peptic ulcer disease is the most common cause of upper gastrointestinal bleeding. The use of Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs) like naproxen is a major risk factor for the development of gastric and duodenal ulcers. B is incorrect as diverticular disease causes lower GI bleeding (usually bright red). C is typically associated with forceful vomiting. D is unlikely in the absence of signs of chronic liver disease or portal hypertension.

question:
A 55 year old man with a known history of liver cirrhosis is seen in the outpatient hepatology clinic. A recent screening gastroscopy revealed the presence of large oesophageal varices that have not previously bled. He has no history of asthma and his heart rate is 72 bpm.

Which medication is most appropriate to prescribe for the primary prophylaxis of variceal haemorrhage in this patient?
feedback: C is correct because non-selective beta-blockers (such as propranolol or carvedilol) are the first-line medical therapy for the primary prophylaxis of variceal bleeding. They work by reducing portal venous pressure. E is incorrect because terlipressin is used in the acute management of an active variceal bleed, not for primary prophylaxis. B is used for peptic ulcers, and D is used for the management of ascites.

question:
A 68 year old man is admitted with haematemesis. He is now haemodynamically stable after initial fluid resuscitation. He has no history of ischaemic heart disease or cerebrovascular disease.

Investigations:
Haemoglobin: 74 g/L (130–175)
Platelets: 160 x 10^9/L (150–400)
INR: 1.1 (0.8–1.2)

According to NICE guidelines for the management of acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding, what is the most appropriate restrictive haemoglobin threshold at which a blood transfusion should be initiated in this patient?
feedback: A is correct because for patients with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding who are not having a massive haemorrhage or do not have significant cardiovascular comorbidities, a restrictive transfusion strategy is recommended. This involves only transfusing when the haemoglobin drops below 70 g/L. B is incorrect as 80 g/L is often the threshold used for patients with pre-existing cardiovascular disease. Higher thresholds (C, D, E) are not supported by current evidence for stable GI bleeds.

question:
A 62 year old man presents to his GP with a six-week history of persistent epigastric discomfort that is poorly relieved by antacids. He also reports an unintended 5kg weight loss and feeling full very quickly after starting a meal.

Investigations:
Haemoglobin: 105 g/L (130–175)
MCV: 74 fL (80–96)
Ferritin: 9 ug/L (15–300)

Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
feedback: D is correct as the patient has 'red flag' symptoms for gastric cancer (new-onset dyspepsia over 55, weight loss, early satiety, and iron deficiency anaemia). In the UK, NICE guidelines mandate an urgent OGD (two-week wait) to visualize the gastric mucosa and obtain biopsies for histological diagnosis. A is useful for gallstones or liver lesions but not for luminal gastric pathology. C is used for staging after a diagnosis is made. E is used for H. pylori detection but is insufficient for ruling out malignancy in the presence of alarm symptoms.

question:
A 71 year old man presents to the Emergency Department with a two-week history of progressively yellowing skin and sclera. He reports that his urine has become very dark and his stools are pale and difficult to flush. He denies any abdominal pain but has lost 7kg in weight over the last two months. On examination, there is a non-tender, palpable mass in the right upper quadrant.

Investigations:
Bilirubin: 115 umol/L (<21)
Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP): 510 U/L (30–130)
Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT): 55 U/L (10–40)

What is the most likely diagnosis?
feedback: D is correct because painless jaundice associated with weight loss and a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier's Law) is highly suggestive of a tumour in the head of the pancreas obstructing the common bile duct. While A (cholangiocarcinoma) also causes obstructive jaundice, it is less common and less likely to present with a palpable gallbladder than a pancreatic head mass. B (gallstones) typically presents with biliary colic (pain). C and E do not typically cause this degree of extrahepatic obstructive jaundice and Courvoisier's sign.

question:
A 58 year old woman with a 40-pack-year smoking history and significant alcohol intake presents to the surgical clinic with difficulty swallowing. She describes a sensation of food 'sticking' in her mid-chest, which started with bread and meat but now includes soft foods. An urgent endoscopy reveals a friable, exophytic mass in the middle third of the oesophagus.

What is the most likely histological type of this tumour?
feedback: E is correct. Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the most likely diagnosis given the patient's strong risk factors (smoking and alcohol) and the location in the middle third of the oesophagus. While Adenocarcinoma (A) is now more common in the UK overall, it is strongly associated with GORD, Barrett's oesophagus, and obesity, and typically occurs in the distal third of the oesophagus. B, C, and D are much rarer types of oesophageal malignancy.

question:
A 48 year old woman is admitted to the emergency department with a 24-hour history of profuse vomiting, central colicky abdominal pain, and failure to pass flatus. She has a history of an open cholecystectomy ten years ago. On examination, she is dehydrated with a heart rate of 110 bpm and a blood pressure of 105/70 mmHg. Her abdomen is distended with tinkling bowel sounds.

Investigations:
Sodium: 136 mmol/L (135–145)
Potassium: 3.1 mmol/L (3.5–5.0)
Chloride: 90 mmol/L (95–105)
Bicarbonate: 35 mmol/L (22–28)
pH: 7.50 (7.35–7.45)

What is the most likely pathophysiological explanation for these biochemical findings?

options.A: Accumulation of lactic acid due to bowel ischaemia
options.B: Loss of gastric hydrochloric acid and potassium due to vomiting
options.C: Movement of potassium into the intracellular space due to acidosis
options.E: Sequestration of bicarbonate in the third space

feedback: The patient has a hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis. This is a classic biochemical complication of high intestinal or gastric outlet obstruction caused by the loss of hydrogen ions (as HCl) and potassium from gastric secretions during vomiting. Lactic acidosis (Option A) would cause a metabolic acidosis, not alkalosis. Acidosis (Option C) typically causes hyperkalaemia, not hypokalaemia.

question:
A 72 year old man presents to his GP with a six-week history of worsening constipation and a feeling of incomplete evacuation. Over the last 48 hours, he has developed significant abdominal distension and has not passed stool or flatus. He has no previous surgical history. On examination, the abdomen is tympanic to percussion and a digital rectal examination reveals an empty rectum.

What is the most likely cause of his obstruction?
feedback: In an elderly patient with no previous abdominal surgery and a subacute history of altered bowel habits (constipation/incomplete evacuation) followed by acute absolute constipation and distension, colorectal carcinoma is the most likely diagnosis. Adhesions (Option A) are the leading cause of small bowel obstruction but usually occur in patients with previous surgery. Sigmoid volvulus (Option D) typically presents more acutely in older, institutionalised patients.

question:
A 65 year old woman presents to the surgical assessment unit with absolute constipation and severe abdominal distension. An initial abdominal X-ray suggests dilated loops of small bowel. The surgical team needs to confirm the diagnosis, identify the transition point, and look for evidence of bowel ischaemia.

Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.C: CT abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast

feedback: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis is the gold standard for diagnosing gastrointestinal obstruction. It is highly sensitive and specific, allowing for the identification of the site (transition point), the cause (e.g., hernia, malignancy), and complications such as bowel wall ischaemia or perforation. Barium enemas (Option A) and colonoscopies (Option B) are less useful in the acute setting of suspected small bowel obstruction.

question:
An 84 year old man with Parkinson's disease is admitted from his care home with massive abdominal distension and discomfort. He has not passed stool for three days. An abdominal X-ray shows a massively dilated loop of large bowel extending from the pelvis to the diaphragm, resembling a 'coffee bean'.

What is the most appropriate initial management for this patient, assuming there are no signs of peritonitis?

options.C: Intravenous fluids and 'drip and suck' management only
options.D: Rigid or flexible sigmoidoscopy and flatus tube insertion

feedback: The 'coffee bean' sign on X-ray is pathognomonic for sigmoid volvulus. In the absence of peritonitis (which would suggest bowel gangrene or perforation), the first-line management is endoscopic decompression using a rigid or flexible sigmoidoscopy and the insertion of a flatus tube to relieve the pressure and untwist the loop. Surgery (Options A and E) is reserved for cases where decompression fails or there is evidence of ischaemia. Laxatives (Option B) are contraindicated in mechanical obstruction.

subtopic: Pathology of Gastritis, Malabsorption and Ulceration
question:
A 45 year old man presents to his GP with a four-week history of burning epigastric pain. The pain is typically worse at night and when he is hungry, but it is often relieved by eating. He has no history of weight loss or dysphagia. He is a smoker of 15 cigarettes per day.

Which of the following organisms is most likely to be associated with this patient's clinical presentation?
feedback: C is the correct answer. The patient's symptoms are classic for a duodenal ulcer (gnawing/burning pain relieved by food). Helicobacter pylori is the primary cause of over 90% of duodenal ulcers and approximately 70-80% of gastric ulcers. Options A and B cause acute diarrhoeal disease. Option D is associated with acute toxin-mediated food poisoning. Option E is the causative agent of Whipple’s disease, a rare cause of malabsorption.
justification: Helicobacter pylori is the most common cause of peptic ulceration in the UK. The symptoms of pain relief with food are highly suggestive of duodenal rather than gastric involvement.

subtopic: Pathology of Gastritis, Malabsorption and Ulceration
question:
A 28 year old woman presents with a six-month history of bloating and increased frequency of pale, voluminous, and difficult-to-flush stools. She also reports feeling persistently tired.

Investigations:
Haemoglobin 105 g/L (120–155)
MCV 74 fL (80–96)
Ferritin 8 µg/L (15–300)
Tissue transglutaminase (tTG) antibodies: Positive

A duodenal biopsy is performed. Which histological feature is most likely to be observed?

options.E: Widened lymphatic channels in the lamina propria

feedback: D is the correct answer. The clinical picture (steatorrhoea, iron deficiency anaemia) and positive tTG antibodies are diagnostic of Coeliac disease. The characteristic histological triad in Coeliac disease is villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. Option A suggests tuberculosis; Option B suggests Ulcerative Colitis; Option C describes Crohn's disease; and Option E is seen in intestinal lymphangiectasia.
justification: Villous atrophy is the hallmark of Coeliac disease-induced malabsorption, leading to a reduced surface area for nutrient absorption, explaining the microcytic anaemia and steatorrhoea.

subtopic: Pathology of Gastritis, Malabsorption and Ulceration
question:
A 72 year old woman is admitted to the emergency department after vomiting bright red blood. She has a history of severe osteoarthritis and takes naproxen 500mg twice daily. 

An urgent gastroscopy reveals a 1.5 cm ulcer in the gastric antrum with evidence of recent haemorrhage. 

What is the primary mechanism by which her medication contributed to this pathology?

options.B: Direct corrosive effect of the drug on the epithelium
options.C: Hypersecretion of gastrin due to feedback inhibition
options.D: Inhibition of the hydrogen-potassium ATPase pump
options.E: Stimulation of histamine release from enterochromaffin-like cells

feedback: A is the correct answer. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like naproxen inhibit the cyclooxygenase (COX-1) enzyme. COX-1 is responsible for the synthesis of prostaglandins (PGE2 and PGI2) which maintain the gastric mucosal barrier by stimulating bicarbonate and mucus secretion and maintaining mucosal blood flow. Option D describes the action of PPIs, not NSAIDs. Option C is seen in gastrinomas (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome).
justification: Prostaglandins are essential for gastric cytoprotection. NSAID-induced inhibition of COX-1 leads to a breakdown of these defences, making the mucosa susceptible to acid-pepsin injury.

subtopic: Pathology of Gastritis, Malabsorption and Ulceration
question:
A 24 year old man presents to the student health clinic with a three-week history of abdominal bloating, excessive flatulence, and greasy, foul-smelling stools. He recently returned from a wild-camping trip in the Peak District where he drank water from local streams.

Which organism is the most likely cause of his chronic diarrhoeal symptoms?
feedback: B is the correct answer. Giardia lamblia is a protozoan parasite that causes 'Giardiasis'. It typically presents with chronic (lasting weeks) watery or fatty diarrhoea (steatorrhoea), bloating, and flatulence. Infection is often linked to contaminated water sources. Options C, D, and E typically cause more acute, self-limiting illnesses. Option A can cause similar symptoms but is more commonly associated with shorter, more watery outbreaks or immunosuppression.
justification: The combination of the camping history (untreated water) and the duration of symptoms with malabsorptive features (greasy stools) is classic for Giardia, which disrupts the brush border of the small intestine.

question:
A 24 year old woman presents to her GP with a 6-month history of bloating, intermittent diarrhoea, and significant lethargy. She mentions that her sister has Type 1 diabetes. On examination, she appears pale but her abdomen is soft and non-tender.

Investigations:
Haemoglobin 105 g/L (115–160)
MCV 72 fL (80–100)
Ferritin 10 µg/L (15–300)

Which is the most appropriate initial investigation to screen for the most likely diagnosis?
feedback: B is the correct answer because IgA anti-tTG is the first-line screening test for Coeliac disease in the UK (NICE guidelines), provided the patient is still consuming gluten. A is incorrect as anti-gliadin antibodies are no longer recommended due to lower sensitivity/specificity. C is incorrect as it is used for lower GI pathology. D is usually reserved for cases where diagnosis is uncertain. E is the gold standard for confirmation but is not the 'initial' screening test.

question: A 42 year old woman has recently been diagnosed with Coeliac disease following a duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia. She is meeting with her GP to discuss the management of her condition. Which of the following grains must she be advised to strictly exclude from her diet?
feedback: A is the correct answer. The treatment for Coeliac disease is a lifelong, strict gluten-free diet. Gluten is found in wheat, barley, and rye. B, C, D, and E are all naturally gluten-free grains/pseudocereals and are safe for patients with Coeliac disease to consume.

question:
A 68 year old woman with a 15-year history of Coeliac disease attends her annual review. She reports that she follows a strict gluten-free diet and her symptoms are well-controlled. However, she is concerned about her risk of long-term complications related to malabsorption. 

Which of the following investigations is most appropriate to assess for a common complication of this condition?
feedback: C is the correct answer. Osteoporosis is a common complication of Coeliac disease due to chronic malabsorption of calcium and Vitamin D; a DEXA scan is recommended to assess bone mineral density. While B is important, it is part of monitoring rather than assessing for the structural complications of malabsorption. D is used to screen for Inflammatory Bowel Disease. E monitors diabetes, which is an association but not a direct complication of malabsorption.

question: A 48 year old man is found to have a duodenal ulcer during an endoscopy for persistent dyspepsia. Biopsies taken from the stomach during the procedure confirm the presence of Helicobacter pylori, concentrated primarily in the antrum. Which pathophysiological change is most directly responsible for the development of his duodenal ulcer?

options.A: Decreased somatostatin release leading to hypergastrinaemia
options.B: Global gastric atrophy leading to achlorhydria
options.C: Increase in protective bicarbonate secretion in the duodenum
options.D: Infection of the Brunner’s glands in the duodenum
options.E: Migration of the bacteria into the bloodstream causing systemic inflammation

feedback: A is correct because H. pylori infection in the antrum leads to a reduction in D-cell somatostatin release. Since somatostatin normally inhibits G-cells, this results in hypergastrinaemia, increased acid secretion from the parietal cells in the gastric body, and subsequent duodenal ulceration. B is incorrect as global atrophy (pangastritis) typically leads to gastric ulcers rather than duodenal ones. C and D are not recognized mechanisms of H. pylori damage.

question: A 72 year old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis is admitted to the medical ward with epigastric pain and melaena. She has been taking naproxen 500mg twice daily for the past three months. Gastroscopy reveals a large gastric ulcer. What is the primary mechanism by which her medication contributed to this condition?

options.A: Activation of the H+/K+ ATPase pump in parietal cells
options.B: Direct caustic injury to the gastric squamous epithelium
options.C: Inhibition of cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1) and reduced prostaglandin E2
options.D: Stimulation of gastrin release from G cells in the antrum
options.E: Upregulation of mucosal nitric oxide synthase

feedback: C is correct because NSAIDs like naproxen inhibit the COX-1 enzyme, which is responsible for the synthesis of prostaglandins (specifically PGE2 and PGI2). These prostaglandins are essential for maintaining the gastric mucosal barrier by stimulating mucus and bicarbonate secretion and maintaining mucosal blood flow. Inhibition leads to increased vulnerability to acid damage. A, D, and E are not mechanisms of NSAID-induced injury. B is incorrect as the stomach is lined with columnar epithelium, not squamous.

question: A 32 year old woman presents to her GP with a 4-week history of epigastric burning pain, which is worse when she is hungry and relieved by eating. She has no weight loss, dysphagia, or persistent vomiting. She has no significant past medical history and takes no regular medications. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.B: Commence a high-dose proton pump inhibitor for 8 weeks
options.C: Perform a 'test and treat' approach for Helicobacter pylori
options.D: Referral to general surgery for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy

feedback: C is correct because according to NICE guidelines, patients under the age of 55 with dyspepsia and no 'alarm' symptoms (red flags like weight loss or dysphagia) should be managed via a 'test and treat' approach for H. pylori using a non-invasive test (such as a C13 urea breath test or stool antigen). A is incorrect as she does not meet the age or red flag criteria for urgent referral. B is incorrect as H. pylori status should be determined before starting long-term PPIs. E is used for suspected Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, which is rare.

question:
A 62 year old man presents to the Emergency Department with sudden onset, excruciating epigastric pain that started 2 hours ago. He describes the pain as 'tearing' and says it is now felt across his entire abdomen. He has a history of indigestion for which he takes over-the-counter antacids. On examination, he is tachycardic (110 bpm) and has a rigid 'board-like' abdomen with generalized guarding.

Investigations:
White cell count 15.5 x 10^9/L (3.0–10.0)
C-reactive protein 88 mg/L (<5)
Haemoglobin 142 g/L (130–175)
Amylase 120 U/L (28–100)

What is the most likely diagnosis?
feedback: C is correct because the sudden onset of severe pain, history of dyspepsia, and the clinical finding of a 'board-like' rigid abdomen (peritonism) are classic for a perforated peptic ulcer. A is less likely as amylase is only mildly elevated (it is usually >3x the upper limit in pancreatitis). B usually presents with colicky RUQ pain without rigidity. D and E are important differentials for sudden pain, but they would not typically cause a rigid abdomen with high inflammatory markers.

question: A 48-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with a 3-month history of intermittent, crampy pain in the right upper quadrant, typically occurring after eating large meals. She has a BMI of 33 and has four children. A diagnosis of gallstones is suspected. Which of the following best describes the primary pathophysiological mechanism leading to the formation of the most common type of gallstone in this patient?

options.A: Bile salt hypersecretion into the gallbladder
options.B: Bilirubin conjugation failure in the liver
options.E: Increased intestinal absorption of bile acids

feedback: C is correct because cholesterol stones are the most common type of gallstone in Western populations, especially in patients with risk factors like female sex, obesity, and multiparity. The process begins with the supersaturation of bile with cholesterol, which then precipitates into crystals. A is incorrect because bile salts actually help solubilise cholesterol; a deficiency in bile salts would promote stones. B refers to pigment stones (bilirubin). D is incorrect as gallbladder hypomotility (not hypermotility) is a risk factor. E is incorrect as decreased recycling of bile acids (e.g., in ileal disease) leads to stones.

question:
A 52-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 6-hour history of constant, severe right upper quadrant pain. He feels feverish and has vomited twice. On examination, his temperature is 38.4°C and his pulse is 95 bpm. There is significant tenderness in the right upper quadrant. When the clinician palpates the right subcostal area during deep inspiration, the patient mid-breath catches his breath due to pain.

Investigations:
White cell count 15.2 x 10^9/L (3.0–10.0)
C-reactive protein 78 mg/L (<5)
Alanine aminotransferase 35 IU/L (10–50)
Bilirubin 14 µmol/L (<17)

What is the most likely diagnosis?
feedback: A is correct because the patient presents with the classic triad of constant RUQ pain, fever, and a positive Murphy’s sign (the catch in breath on palpation). The raised inflammatory markers (WBC and CRP) support an inflammatory/infectious process rather than simple biliary colic. B is incorrect as there is no jaundice (normal bilirubin) or Charcot's triad. C is incorrect as biliary colic pain is typically intermittent and not associated with fever or raised inflammatory markers. D refers to a mechanical bowel obstruction caused by a stone. E would typically present with more generalised peritonitis and a rigid abdomen.

question:
A 65-year-old man is reviewed in the surgical outpatient clinic. He recently underwent an abdominal ultrasound scan for the investigation of vague bloating, which incidentally identified two 1cm gallstones within the gallbladder. The gallbladder wall was not thickened and the common bile duct was of normal calibre. He has never had episodes of right upper quadrant pain or jaundice. He has a history of well-controlled hypertension and takes amlodipine.

What is the most appropriate management for his gallstones?
feedback: C is correct because most patients with asymptomatic gallstones found incidentally do not require treatment. The risk of developing symptoms or complications is low (about 1-2% per year). A is incorrect as surgery is generally reserved for symptomatic patients. B is used for ductal stones, not gallbladder stones. D is rarely used in modern practice for gallstones. E has limited efficacy and is only occasionally used in patients unfit for surgery who have specific types of small, radiolucent stones.

question:
A 58-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital with a 4-hour history of sudden-onset, severe epigastric pain that radiates through to her back. She has no history of alcohol excess. On examination, she is distressed and tachycardic. Her abdomen is tender in the epigastric region with no guarding.

Investigations:
Amylase 1650 U/L (28–100)
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 195 IU/L (10–50)
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) 130 IU/L (25–115)
Bilirubin 19 µmol/L (<17)

Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the underlying cause of this presentation?
feedback: E is correct because the patient has acute pancreatitis (suggested by the severe epigastric pain and amylase >3x upper limit). The lack of alcohol history and the elevated ALT (>3x upper limit) strongly suggest a gallstone etiology. Transabdominal ultrasound is the first-line investigation to look for gallstones as the underlying cause. A is not useful for diagnosis. B is useful for assessing severity/complications of pancreatitis but not necessarily the first-line for finding the cause (stones). C and D are more invasive or secondary investigations used if the ultrasound is inconclusive or if ductal stones are specifically suspected.

question:
A 24 year old woman presents to her GP with a six-month history of crampy lower abdominal pain and bloating. She reports that the pain is often relieved by defecation. Over the last two months, she has noticed her stools have become harder and less frequent, occurring only twice a week. She has not lost weight, has no family history of bowel cancer, and denies seeing any blood in her stool.

Investigations:
Haemoglobin: 132 g/L (115–160)
C-reactive protein (CRP): 2 mg/L (<5)
Tissue transglutaminase (tTG) antibody: Negative

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
feedback: C is correct because the patient meets the Rome IV criteria for Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS): chronic abdominal pain related to defecation and a change in stool frequency/form for at least 6 months, in the absence of 'red flags' (weight loss, blood) and with normal inflammatory markers (CRP) and negative coeliac serology (tTG). A and B are less likely given the normal CRP and negative tTG. D is ruled out by the lack of bloody diarrhoea and normal CRP.
justification: IBS is a functional disorder diagnosed clinically using the Rome IV criteria when organic pathology has been excluded.

question:
A 22 year old medical student is recently diagnosed with Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS). During a consultation, she asks her GP why she experiences significant pain from normal levels of intestinal gas that her peers do not seem to notice. The GP explains the current understanding of the biopsychosocial model of functional gut disorders.

Which of the following mechanisms best explains this patient's symptoms?

options.A: Autoimmune destruction of the myenteric plexus
options.B: Increased intestinal permeability causing systemic inflammation
options.D: T-cell mediated reaction to gluten peptides

feedback: E is correct because visceral hypersensitivity (an increased sensation of pain in response to normal stimuli like gut distension) is a hallmark of functional gut disorders. A describes Achalasia/Hirschsprung-like pathology. B refers to the 'leaky gut' hypothesis but is not the primary mechanism of IBS pain. C describes Crohn's disease. D describes Coeliac disease.
justification: Visceral hypersensitivity involves altered processing of sensory information from the gut to the brain, leading to lower pain thresholds.

question:
A 34 year old man with a known diagnosis of diarrhoea-predominant Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS-D) returns to the clinic. He has attempted a low FODMAP (Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monosaccharides, and Polyols) diet for three months with some improvement in bloating, but he still struggles with frequent, loose stools and urgency that interfere with his work as a delivery driver.

Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological treatment for his diarrhoea?
feedback: D is correct because loperamide is the first-line antimotility agent recommended for the symptomatic relief of diarrhoea in IBS-D. A (Amitriptyline) is a second-line treatment (TCA) for pain. B (Ispaghula) is a bulking agent used for constipation. C (Linaclotide) is used for moderate-to-severe constipation-predominant IBS. E is a steroid used for IBD, not functional disorders.
justification: NICE guidelines recommend antimotility agents as the first-line choice for managing diarrhoea in patients with IBS.

question:
A 29 year old woman presents to the GP with a 4-month history of intermittent abdominal bloating and loose stools. She has no weight loss, no nocturnal diarrhoea, and no blood in the stool. Her mother has Crohn’s disease. To help differentiate between a functional disorder like Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), the GP orders a stool test.

Which of the following investigations is most specific for identifying intestinal inflammation in this context?
feedback: A is correct because faecal calprotectin is a protein released by neutrophils during intestinal inflammation; it is highly sensitive for IBD and helps distinguish it from functional disorders like IBS. B and C look for blood, which is a screening tool for malignancy or polyps rather than a specific marker for inflammation. D and E are used to rule out infectious causes of diarrhoea.
justification: Faecal calprotectin is the standard non-invasive test used in primary care to rule out IBD in patients under 40 with IBS symptoms.

question:
A 52 year old man presents to the Emergency Department with sudden onset, excruciating upper abdominal pain that has now become generalized. He has a history of chronic indigestion for which he takes over-the-counter antacids. 

On examination, his blood pressure is 105/65 mmHg, pulse rate 115 bpm (60–100) and temperature 37.8°C (36.0–37.5). His abdomen is "board-like" with generalized rigidity and guarding. Bowel sounds are absent.

Which is the most likely diagnosis?
feedback: D is correct because the sudden onset of 'board-like' rigidity (generalized peritonitis) in a patient with a history of dyspepsia is classic for a perforated peptic ulcer. Pancreatitis (B) usually presents with pain radiating to the back and typically lacks the immediate 'board-like' rigidity. Acute cholecystitis (A) usually presents with localized right upper quadrant pain and Murphy's sign. Mesenteric ischaemia (C) often presents with pain out of proportion to clinical findings initially, without immediate rigidity. Small bowel obstruction (E) presents with distension and tinkling bowel sounds rather than generalized rigidity.

question:
A 60 year old woman with a known history of liver cirrhosis and ascites is admitted to the medical ward with increased abdominal distension and mild confusion. She has no vomiting or diarrhoea. Her temperature is 38.1°C (36.0–37.5).

Investigations:
Bilirubin 55 µmol/L (3–17)
Albumin 22 g/L (35–50)
Ascitic fluid neutrophil count: 420 cells/mm³ (<250)
Ascitic fluid Gram stain: Gram-negative bacilli seen

Which organism is the most likely cause of this presentation?
feedback: B is correct because Escherichia coli is the most common organism isolated in Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP), followed by Klebsiella species. SBP is defined by an ascitic neutrophil count > 250 cells/mm³. Bacteroides fragilis (A) is an anaerobe; anaerobes are rare in SBP because the high oxygen tension of ascitic fluid inhibits their growth. S. pneumoniae (E) is a recognized cause but is less common in adults with cirrhosis than E. coli.

question:
A 22 year old man presents to his GP with a 12-hour history of abdominal pain. The pain initially started as a dull ache around his umbilicus but has now moved to the right iliac fossa, where it is sharp and significantly worsened by coughing or movement. On examination, there is localized tenderness and rebound tenderness at McBurney's point.

What is the anatomical basis for the transition of the pain to being sharp and well-localized in the right iliac fossa?

options.B: Irritation of the parietal peritoneum supplied by somatic nerves
options.C: Irritation of the visceral peritoneum supplied by autonomic nerves
options.D: Referred pain from the T10 dermatome

feedback: B is correct. Initial appendicitis pain is visceral, caused by distension of the appendix, and is poorly localized to the midline (periumbilical T10) via autonomic fibres. As the inflammation spreads to involve the adjacent parietal peritoneum, the pain becomes somatic. The parietal peritoneum is supplied by somatic nerves (e.g., the intercostal nerves), which allow for precise localization, sharp character, and exacerbation by movement (peritonism).

question:
A 65 year old man is hospitalized with decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis. He develops a low-grade fever and abdominal discomfort. Paracentesis is performed to investigate for Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP).

Investigations:
Ascitic fluid neutrophil count: 310 cells/mm³ (<250)
Creatinine: 110 µmol/L (60–110)

He has no known drug allergies. What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological management?
feedback: A is correct. Third-generation cephalosporins such as IV cefotaxime are the empirical treatment of choice for SBP as they cover the most likely gram-negative (e.g., E. coli) and gram-positive (e.g., Streptococci) pathogens. Metronidazole (C) is for anaerobes, which are rarely involved. While quinolones (D) can be used for prophylaxis, IV cephalosporins are first-line for acute treatment. Gentamicin (B) is avoided in cirrhosis due to the high risk of nephrotoxicity and hepatorenal syndrome.

question: A 54 year old man presents to his GP complaining of increasing abdominal girth over the last three weeks. He has a history of alcohol excess and was previously told he has 'scarring of the liver'. On examination, he appears jaundiced and has several spider naevi. The GP performs a physical examination of the abdomen to confirm the presence of fluid. Which of the following physical examination findings is the most sensitive for the detection of ascites?
feedback: D is correct because shifting dullness is generally considered the most sensitive physical examination sign for detecting ascites (sensitivity approximately 83%), although its specificity is lower than the fluid thrill. A is incorrect because while bulging flanks occur in ascites, they are less sensitive and can be seen in obesity. B is incorrect because a fluid thrill is highly specific but only present in massive ascites, making it less sensitive for smaller volumes. C is incorrect as the puddle sign is difficult to perform and less commonly used in modern practice compared to shifting dullness. E is incorrect as distension is a non-specific observation.

question:
A 68 year old woman is admitted to the medical ward for investigation of new-onset ascites. She has lost 6kg in weight over the last two months and reports early satiety. A diagnostic paracentesis is performed, and blood samples are taken simultaneously. 

Investigations:
Serum albumin: 32 g/L (35–50)
Ascitic fluid albumin: 25 g/L
Ascitic fluid cytology: Awaiting result

Which of the following is the most likely cause of her ascites?
feedback: D is correct because the Serum-Ascites Albumin Gradient (SAAG) is 7 g/L (32 minus 25). A SAAG < 11 g/L indicates a low gradient (exudative-like), which is characteristic of conditions not related to portal hypertension. Common causes of a low SAAG include peritoneal carcinomatosis, tuberculosis, and nephrotic syndrome. A, B, C, and E are all causes of a high SAAG (≥ 11 g/L), as they are associated with increased hydrostatic pressure in the portal venous system or hepatic sinusoids.

question: A 52 year old man with a known diagnosis of compensated cirrhosis attends the hepatology clinic. He has developed moderate (Grade 2) ascites. He has no history of gastrointestinal bleeding or encephalopathy. His renal function is normal. He has already been advised on a low-sodium diet, but the ascites has not improved. What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological treatment for this patient?

options.B: Large volume paracentesis with albumin cover

feedback: D is correct because aldosterone antagonists, such as spironolactone, are the first-line diuretic treatment for ascites secondary to cirrhosis. This is because the underlying pathophysiology involves secondary hyperaldosteronism leading to sodium retention. A is incorrect because loop diuretics like furosemide are typically less effective as monotherapy in cirrhosis and are usually added to spironolactone. B is incorrect as paracentesis is reserved for Grade 3 (tense) ascites or refractory cases. C is incorrect as steroids are not used to treat ascites. E is incorrect as TIPS is a second-line intervention for refractory ascites.

question: A 61 year old man with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis and chronic ascites is brought to the Emergency Department with a 24-hour history of vague abdominal pain and new-onset confusion. On examination, he is febrile (38.2°C) and has mild generalized abdominal tenderness without guarding. A diagnostic ascitic tap is performed. Which of the following results would most strongly support a diagnosis of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP)?

options.E: Positive Gram stain for Gram-negative rods

feedback: C is correct because the diagnosis of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is primarily based on an ascitic fluid absolute neutrophil count (ANC) of ≥ 250 cells/mm³. A and B are more characteristic of secondary peritonitis (e.g., gut perforation). D is incorrect as SBP usually occurs in the context of low-protein ascites (< 15 g/L), as low opsonic activity predisposes to infection. E is incorrect because Gram stains of ascitic fluid are frequently negative in SBP due to the low concentration of bacteria; treatment is started based on the neutrophil count while awaiting cultures.

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
question: A 68-year-old woman with a history of hypercholesterolaemia and type 2 diabetes is seen by her GP for a medication review. The GP notes that she has not been collecting her statin prescription regularly. When asked, the patient explains she is worried about potential liver damage she read about online. The GP acknowledges her concerns, provides evidence-based information on risks versus benefits, and they mutually agree to continue the medication with an extra blood test in two months to reassure her. Which of the following terms best describes this collaborative approach to medicine taking?
feedback: C is correct because concordance is a process where the patient and the clinician work together to reach an agreement about care, acknowledging the patient's values and beliefs. This differs from compliance (the patient simply following the doctor's orders) and adherence (the extent to which the patient's behaviour matches the agreed recommendations). Deprescribing is the process of supervised medication withdrawal. Polypharmacy refers to the use of multiple medications by a single patient.

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
question: A 52-year-old man presents to his GP feeling increasingly stressed and isolated following a divorce. He has a BMI of 32 kg/m² and a family history of ischaemic heart disease. He is reluctant to start medications for his mood or weight. The GP suggests 'social prescribing' by referring him to a local community-led 'walking group' that meets in a nearby forest. Which of the following is a recognised 'con' (disadvantage) of this type of intervention compared to standard pharmacological treatment?

options.A: Higher risk of systemic pharmacological side effects
options.B: Increased likelihood of patient physiological dependency
options.C: Lack of standardized regulation and variable local availability
options.D: Limited impact on the social determinants of health
options.E: Reduced patient involvement in the decision-making process

feedback: C is correct. While social prescribing (including green prescribing like walking in nature) has many benefits, a significant disadvantage is that services are often provided by the voluntary or community sector, meaning they are not as strictly regulated as the pharmaceutical industry and their availability can vary significantly between different geographical regions ('postcode lottery'). Options A and B are disadvantages of medication, not social prescribing. Social prescribing is specifically designed to address social determinants (D) and increase patient involvement (E).

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
question:
A 29-year-old woman attends her GP surgery for a scheduled 6-week postnatal check with her healthy infant. During the consultation, the GP wishes to screen for postnatal depression as part of the routine assessment. The mother mentions that she has been feeling quite tired, but attributes this to the baby's sleep pattern. 

Which of the following represents the most appropriate initial screening approach for depression in this setting according to NICE guidelines?

options.A: Administer the 10-item Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)
options.B: Ask the two 'Whooley' questions regarding mood and interest
options.C: Perform a formal Mental State Examination (MSE)
options.D: Request a blood test for thyroid function and iron levels
options.E: Use the GAD-7 tool to assess for comorbid anxiety disorders

feedback: The 'Whooley' questions are the recommended initial screening tool for depression in the postnatal period in primary care. They consist of asking: 'During the past month, have you often been bothered by feeling down, depressed or hopeless?' and 'During the past month, have you often been bothered by having little interest or pleasure in doing things?'. If a woman responds positively to these, a more formal tool like the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) or PHQ-9 should be used. While tired mothers may need blood tests for physical causes (Option D), it is not the primary screening method for postnatal depression. A formal MSE (Option C) is usually reserved for those who screen positive or present with more severe symptoms.
feedback_text: B is correct because the Whooley questions are the validated first-line screening tool for depression in the postnatal period. A is incorrect because the EPDS is typically used as a second-step assessment if the initial screen is positive. C is incorrect as a full MSE is a diagnostic rather than a screening tool. D is incorrect as it screens for physical fatigue causes, not depression. E is incorrect as GAD-7 screens specifically for anxiety.

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
question:
A 24-year-old woman who gave birth 5 days ago is seen by her GP. She has been trying to breastfeed but is finding it extremely painful due to cracked nipples and is worried her baby is not getting enough milk. She expresses significant guilt and tearfully asks if it would be 'wrong' to switch to infant formula. 

In accordance with providing non-judgmental feeding advice, what is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Advise that formula feeding is associated with higher rates of childhood obesity and she should continue breastfeeding for at least 6 months.
options.B: Explain that breastfeeding is the 'gold standard' and offer to prescribe nipple cream so she can continue.
options.C: Inform her that many mothers experience this and that switching to formula is a valid and safe choice if she feels it is right for her and her baby.
options.D: Suggest that her guilt is a sign of postnatal depression and refer her immediately to the perinatal mental health team.
options.E: Tell her that breast milk is the only way to provide the baby with necessary antibodies and formula should only be used as a last resort.

feedback: Medical professionals should provide non-judgmental, evidence-based information that supports the mother's choice and well-being. Acknowledging that formula is a safe alternative (Option C) respects maternal autonomy and can alleviate the psychological distress associated with feeding difficulties. Options A, B, and E, while highlighting the benefits of breastfeeding, are judgmental and can exacerbate guilt and pressure, potentially damaging the doctor-patient relationship and the mother's mental health. While breastfeeding has many benefits, a mother's mental health and informed choice are paramount.
feedback_text: C is correct as it validates the mother's concerns and supports her autonomy in a non-judgmental way. A and E are judgmental and use pressure tactics. B dismisses the severity of her distress and focuses only on a physical fix. D over-pathologises common feeding-related distress without first addressing the feeding issue.

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
question: A 45-year-old man attends a GP surgery as a walk-in patient. He has been sleeping in a night shelter for the past two months and presents with a productive cough, evening fevers, and a 4kg weight loss over the last six weeks. He explains that he tried to register at a different practice previously but was told he could not be seen because he did not have a utility bill to prove his address or a passport. Which category of barrier to healthcare is this patient primarily describing?
feedback: Administrative barrier. Feedback: Administrative barriers are a significant hurdle for homeless populations. Despite NHS England guidance stating that a lack of fixed address or identification is not a valid reason to refuse GP registration, many patients are still turned away due to internal practice policies requiring these documents. Attitudinal barriers refer to the perceived or actual stigma from staff. Financial barriers relate to the cost of travel or prescriptions. Communication barriers might involve literacy or language issues, and physical barriers involve the geographic location or opening hours of a service.

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
question: A 29-year-old woman is being discharged from the Emergency Department after treatment for a minor injury. During the social history, she reveals that she has no permanent residence and has been 'sofa surfing' at various acquaintances' houses for the last three weeks. She notes that she often has to leave at short notice and does not know where she will sleep tomorrow. According to the European Typology of Homelessness and Housing Exclusion (ETHOS), which category of homelessness does this patient's current situation best fall under?
feedback: Insecure housing. Feedback: The ETHOS typology classifies homelessness into four main categories: Rooflessness (living rough), Houselessness (living in shelters/temporary institutions), Insecure housing (living in temporary accommodation with family/friends 'sofa surfing', or under threat of eviction/violence), and Inadequate housing (living in unfit or overcrowded conditions). Sofa surfing is a classic example of insecure housing. Statutory homelessness is a legal definition used by local authorities in the UK to determine if they have a duty to rehouse someone, but it is not a category within the ETHOS framework.

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
question: A 72 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department by his daughter with a sudden onset of weakness. On examination, he has significant weakness in his right leg (power 2/5) compared to his right arm (power 4/5). He is also noted to be unusually quiet and has been incontinent of urine since the symptoms started. A CT head excludes intracranial haemorrhage. Which of the following blood vessels is most likely to be occluded?
feedback: Correct: A. The clinical presentation of contralateral lower limb weakness exceeding upper limb weakness, combined with urinary incontinence and frontal lobe signs (apathy/personality changes), is classic for an Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA) territory stroke. Because the symptoms are on the right side, the lesion must be in the left hemisphere. Left Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA) strokes (Option B) typically cause weakness that affects the face and arm more than the leg. Left Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA) strokes (Option C) usually present with visual field defects such as homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. Right-sided vessel occlusions (Options D and E) would cause left-sided motor deficits.

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
question: A 68 year old woman is admitted to the stroke unit following an acute ischaemic stroke. A CT head performed on arrival excluded haemorrhage. She was not eligible for thrombolysis as she presented 8 hours after the onset of her symptoms. She has a history of hypertension and takes ramipril. Her observations are: BP 155/92 mmHg, Heart Rate 78 bpm, Temperature 36.8°C, Blood Glucose 5.4 mmol/L [3.9 - 5.8]. Her swallow screen is safe for oral medications. According to NICE guidelines, what is the most appropriate immediate antiplatelet management for this patient?
feedback: Correct: B. For patients with an acute ischaemic stroke who have had a primary intracerebral haemorrhage excluded by imaging, NICE guidelines (NG128) recommend Aspirin 300 mg daily for 14 days. This should be started as soon as possible (within 24 hours). Aspirin 75 mg (Option A) is a maintenance dose and is insufficient for acute treatment. Clopidogrel 75 mg (Option C) is the standard for long-term secondary prevention after the initial 14-day period of aspirin. Alteplase (Option D) is the thrombolytic agent used if the patient presents within 4.5 hours. Warfarin (Option E) is not used in the acute management of ischaemic stroke unless there is a specific indication like atrial fibrillation, and even then, it is usually delayed.

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
question:
A 64-year-old male construction worker presents to his GP with a 6-month history of worsening shortness of breath on exertion and a persistent cough productive of clear sputum. He has a 45-pack-year smoking history. On examination, he is tachypnoeic at rest with a respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute, and hyperresonance is noted on chest percussion. Spirometry is performed to confirm the suspected diagnosis. 

Which of the following spirometric findings is most characteristic of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)?

options.A: FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.60 after the administration of a bronchodilator
options.B: FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.85 with a Total Lung Capacity (TLC) below the 5th percentile
options.C: FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.65 which increases to 0.80 following 400mcg of inhaled salbutamol
options.D: Peak Expiratory Flow (PEF) variability of 25% over a two-week monitoring period
options.E: Transfer factor of the lung for carbon monoxide (TLCO) significantly above the reference range

feedback: A is correct because the hallmark of COPD is persistent, largely irreversible airflow obstruction, defined as a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio of less than 0.70. B describes a restrictive pattern (normal ratio, low volumes), which is more typical of interstitial lung disease or obesity. C describes significant reversibility of airflow obstruction, which is the diagnostic hallmark of asthma rather than COPD. D describes PEF variability, which is also used to diagnose asthma. E is incorrect as emphysema (a component of COPD) typically causes a decrease in TLCO due to alveolar wall destruction and loss of surface area for gas exchange; an increased TLCO can be seen in asthma or pulmonary haemorrhage.

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
question:
A 71-year-old woman with a diagnosis of COPD is reviewed in the respiratory clinic. She currently uses a salbutamol inhaler (SABA) as required but reports that she is still breathless on most days and is unable to keep up with people of her own age (mMRC Grade 2). She has not had any acute exacerbations in the past 12 months. Her blood results show an eosinophil count of 0.1 x 10^9/L [Reference: 0.0–0.4 x 10^9/L]. 

In accordance with NICE guidelines, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in her pharmacological management?

options.B: Add a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) and a long-acting beta2-agonist (LABA)
options.C: Add a long-acting beta2-agonist (LABA) and an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)
options.E: Prescribe a course of oral prednisolone and prophylactic antibiotics

feedback: B is correct because NICE guidelines (NG115) recommend the addition of LABA + LAMA combination therapy for patients who remain symptomatic despite SABA/SAMA use and who do not have 'asthmatic features' or a high eosinophil count. C is incorrect because LABA + ICS is recommended for those with asthmatic features (e.g., high eosinophils or diurnal variation). A is incorrect because ICS should not be used as monotherapy in COPD. D is incorrect as LTOT is indicated for chronic hypoxia (PaO2 < 7.3 kPa), which is not suggested here. E is incorrect as this describes the management of an acute exacerbation, not the escalation of stable maintenance therapy.

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
question:
A 54-year-old man attends his GP surgery for the results of a routine health check. He has no significant past medical history and feels well. His BMI is 31 kg/m2 and his blood pressure is 138/86 mmHg. His HbA1c is reported as 44 mmol/mol [Reference range: <42 mmol/mol]. 

How should this result be explained to the patient according to current clinical guidelines?

options.A: His blood sugar is in the diabetic range and he must start Metformin immediately
options.B: His blood sugar is higher than normal, placing him at high risk of developing Type 2 diabetes
options.C: This is a normal result for his age and no further action or follow-up is required
options.D: This result indicates he has Type 1 diabetes and requires an urgent referral to secondary care
options.E: He has developed 'sugar intolerance' and must strictly avoid all carbohydrates from now on

feedback: B is correct because an HbA1c between 42-47 mmol/mol indicates non-diabetic hyperglycaemia, also known as pre-diabetes. This means the patient is at high risk of developing Type 2 diabetes and should be offered lifestyle advice and enrollment in a prevention programme. A is incorrect as the threshold for a diagnosis of Type 2 diabetes is an HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol or higher. C is incorrect as the result is above the normal range and requires intervention. D is incorrect as Type 1 diabetes usually presents with acute osmotic symptoms and lower BMI, and the HbA1c threshold is the same. E is incorrect as 'sugar intolerance' is not a clinical term and absolute avoidance of all carbohydrates is not recommended medical advice; instead, a balanced diet with low glycaemic index foods is advised.

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
question:
A 68-year-old woman with a 10-year history of Type 2 diabetes attends the surgery for her annual diabetic review. She mentions that she has been feeling well but sometimes experiences 'pins and needles' in her toes at night. 

Which of the following assessments is a mandatory component of the annual diabetic review specifically to screen for microvascular complications?

options.C: Cognitive screening using the Abbreviated Mental Test Score (AMTS)
options.D: Measurement of the albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR) in a urine sample
options.E: Total cholesterol to HDL ratio blood test

feedback: D is correct because annual screening for diabetic nephropathy (a microvascular complication) involves testing for albuminuria using the urinary albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR) alongside eGFR. A and B are incorrect as they relate to macrovascular disease (cardiovascular and cerebrovascular), which while important, are not the primary 'microvascular' screens. C is incorrect as cognitive screening is not a standard mandatory component of the basic annual diabetic review. E is incorrect as lipid profiles screen for cardiovascular risk (macrovascular) rather than microvascular damage.

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
question: A 72-year-old man presents to his GP complaining of intermittent palpitations and fatigue over the last month. He has a past medical history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. On examination, his pulse is irregularly irregular at 92 bpm and his blood pressure is 148/92 mmHg. An ECG confirms a diagnosis of atrial fibrillation. His ORBIT score is 1 (low risk). Using the CHA2DS2-VASc tool, what is the most appropriate next step in his management regarding stroke prevention?

options.D: No anticoagulation is required as his score is too low

feedback: C is correct. The patient's CHA2DS2-VASc score is 3 (Age 65-74 = 1, Hypertension = 1, Diabetes = 1). In men, NICE guidelines recommend offering anticoagulation (preferably a Direct Oral Anticoagulant/DOAC like Apixaban) if the score is 2 or more. A and B are incorrect because antiplatelets are not recommended for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation. D is incorrect as a score of 3 necessitates treatment. E is a rate-control agent (beta-blocker) which treats the symptoms/rate but does not provide stroke prophylaxis.

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
question: A 58-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 3-hour history of rapid, regular palpitations and mild shortness of breath. She has no significant past medical history. An ECG is performed which shows a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia with a ventricular rate of 150 bpm. There is a distinct 'saw-tooth' appearance of the baseline in the inferior leads (II, III, and aVF). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
feedback: B is correct. Atrial Flutter is characterized by a regular 'saw-tooth' baseline (F-waves), often seen most clearly in the inferior leads. A regular ventricular rate of exactly 150 bpm is a classic presentation of Atrial Flutter with 2:1 conduction (where the atrial rate is 300 bpm). A is incorrect as Atrial Fibrillation is irregularly irregular. C involves a total dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes. D is characterized by a PR interval >200ms with a 1:1 ratio. E would show normal P-wave morphology preceding every QRS complex and rarely sustains a rate of exactly 150 bpm in a resting adult without a specific trigger.

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
question:
A 74-year-old man is brought to the memory clinic by his wife. She reports that over the last 14 months his memory has declined, but she is particularly struck by how his level of confusion varies; some days he is relatively lucid, while on others he is very disoriented. He has also begun reporting seeing 'strange children' playing in their hallway who are not there. On examination, the GP notes a shuffling gait and a resting 'pill-rolling' tremor in his right hand. 

Blood tests show:
TSH: 2.2 mIU/L (0.4–4.0 mIU/L)
Vitamin B12: 380 ng/L (200–900 ng/L)
Corrected Calcium: 2.35 mmol/L (2.20–2.60 mmol/L)

What is the most likely diagnosis?
feedback: B is correct because the clinical triad of fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, and spontaneous motor features of parkinsonism (tremor, shuffling gait) is characteristic of Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB). A is incorrect because Alzheimer’s typically presents with early prominent memory loss without early hallucinations or motor signs. C is incorrect as Frontotemporal dementia usually presents with early personality change or language deficit. D is incorrect as while it causes gait changes, it is typically associated with urinary incontinence and 'wacky' (cognitive) changes without specific visual hallucinations. E is incorrect as it typically follows a stepwise decline associated with vascular risk factors or stroke events.

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
question:
An 81-year-old woman with a three-year history of moderate Alzheimer's disease is seen in the GP surgery. Her cognitive function has declined to the point where she is assessed as lacking the mental capacity to consent to a proposed elective hip replacement for severe osteoarthritis. Her daughter states that she has the legal authority to make healthcare decisions on her mother's behalf. 

Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 (England and Wales), which of the following legal instruments must be in place and registered to allow the daughter to provide consent for this surgery?

options.B: Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA) for Health and Welfare
options.C: Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA) for Property and Financial Affairs
options.E: The daughter's status as 'Next of Kin'

feedback: B is correct. A Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA) for Health and Welfare allows a donor to appoint an attorney to make decisions about their healthcare and personal welfare only when the donor lacks the capacity to do so themselves. It must be registered with the Office of the Public Guardian. C is incorrect because a Property and Financial Affairs LPA only grants authority over money, property, and assets, not medical treatments. A is incorrect as an ADRT is used by a patient to refuse specific treatments in advance. D is incorrect as an Ordinary Power of Attorney is only valid while the donor still has mental capacity. E is incorrect because 'Next of Kin' has no legal standing to consent to or refuse medical treatment for an adult in the UK.

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
question:
A 17-year-old girl is brought to the GP surgery by her mother. Her mother is concerned that she has become increasingly withdrawn, has stopped eating meals with the family, and spends several hours every day exercising in her room. On examination, the patient is wearing multiple layers of loose-fitting clothing despite the warm weather. Her heart rate is 46 bpm and her blood pressure is 92/58 mmHg. Her body mass index (BMI) is calculated at 15.8 kg/m².

Which of the following physical examination findings is most likely to be present in this patient?
feedback: A is correct because Lanugo hair (fine, downy hair growth on the trunk and limbs) is a common physiological adaptation to extreme weight loss and malnutrition in Anorexia Nervosa, thought to be the body's attempt to insulate itself against heat loss. B is incorrect as parotid gland enlargement is typically associated with frequent self-induced vomiting, more common in Bulimia Nervosa. C is incorrect as while oedema can occur in severe malnutrition or refeeding, lanugo hair is a more characteristic physical sign of the restrictive state. D is incorrect as Russell's sign (calluses on the knuckles) is a sign of self-induced vomiting. E is incorrect as patients with anorexia nervosa typically exhibit bradycardia (as seen in this patient's HR of 46 bpm) rather than tachycardia.

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
question:
A 20-year-old woman with a long-standing history of restrictive anorexia nervosa is admitted to a medical ward for nutritional rehabilitation. Her BMI is 13.5 kg/m². On the third day of supervised refeeding, she develops profound muscle weakness and confusion. 

Blood results are obtained:
Sodium: 138 mmol/L (135–145 mmol/L)
Potassium: 3.1 mmol/L (3.5–5.0 mmol/L)
Phosphate: 0.45 mmol/L (0.8–1.5 mmol/L)
Magnesium: 0.60 mmol/L (0.7–1.0 mmol/L)
Glucose: 4.2 mmol/L (4.0–7.0 mmol/L)

Which of the following is the primary physiological mechanism responsible for the serum phosphate level seen in this patient?

options.A: Excessive renal excretion of phosphate due to metabolic alkalosis
options.B: Inadequate dietary phosphate content in the refeeding formula
options.C: Insulin-mediated shift of phosphate from extracellular to intracellular compartments
options.D: Malabsorption of phosphate due to chronic intestinal villous atrophy
options.E: Reduced parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion leading to phosphate loss

feedback: C is correct because the patient is experiencing Refeeding Syndrome. When nutrition (especially carbohydrates) is reintroduced after a period of starvation, the body moves from a catabolic to an anabolic state. This causes a surge in insulin, which stimulates the movement of glucose, phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into the cells. In a person with already depleted total-body stores, this shift causes a dangerous drop in serum levels. Hypophosphataemia is the hallmark of this syndrome. A, B, D, and E are incorrect as they do not describe the primary mechanism of refeeding syndrome; the shift is driven by the hormonal response to glucose/insulin, not primary renal loss or malabsorption.

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
question:
A 65-year-old man presents to his GP with a 4-month history of worsening urinary symptoms. He reports that he often has to wait for several seconds for his urinary stream to start and notes that the flow is significantly weaker than it used to be. He also complains of 'dribbling' at the end of micturition.

Which of the following symptoms, if elicited on further history taking, would be classified as a 'storage' symptom rather than a 'voiding' symptom?
feedback: Nocturia is classified as a storage (or irritative) symptom. Storage symptoms include frequency, urgency, nocturia, and urgency incontinence. Hesitancy (A), intermittency (B), post-micturition dribble (D), and straining (E) are all classified as voiding (or obstructive) symptoms, typically associated with conditions such as benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) that cause bladder outlet obstruction.

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
question:
A 71-year-old man presents to a primary care clinic with a 3-month history of increased urinary frequency, nocturia, and a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying. He has a 45-pack-year smoking history and worked in the dye industry for 30 years. He denies any pain on urination.

When performing a history for lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS), which of the following questions is most important for identifying a 'red flag' for underlying malignancy in this patient?

options.A: Have you noticed any blood in your urine?
options.B: Do you find it difficult to start your stream?
options.C: Do you have any lower back or hip pain?
options.D: How many times do you wake up at night to pass urine?
options.E: Is the flow of urine interrupted or stop-start?

feedback: Painless visible hematuria (blood in the urine) is a major 'red flag' for urological malignancy, particularly bladder cancer, especially in an elderly patient with significant risk factors like a smoking history and occupational exposure to dyes. While back pain (C) can be a red flag for metastatic prostate cancer, painless hematuria is the most direct indicator for primary bladder or renal tract malignancy. Options B, D, and E relate to standard LUTS assessment (voiding and storage) but are not specific red flags for malignancy.

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
subtopic: Liver disease, Hepatitis and Sexual health
question:
A 56-year-old man presents to the GP complaining of increasing abdominal girth and mild discomfort. He has a 20-year history of heavy alcohol consumption. On examination, the GP notes jaundice, spider naevi on the chest, and a fluid thrill on abdominal percussion. Blood results are as follows:

Bilirubin: 58 µmol/L (5-21 µmol/L)
Albumin: 24 g/L (35-50 g/L)
ALT: 72 U/L (5-40 U/L)
Prothrombin Time (PT): 19 seconds (11-14 seconds)
